Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, it is a delight for me to join this timely discussion on using technology to open and safeguard safe space for women to have their voices heard in public life. As we have heard throughout this Congress and this morning, digital technologies have transformed our societies dramatically in recent years. They have opened unprecedented opportunities for connection, innovation, civil engagement, and economic empowerment. And for many women, digital platforms have created opportunities to speak, to organize, to lead, and to advocate for positive change at every level, from the local to the global. But every door that technology opens can also open a door for harm to enter. The digital space is increasingly being used to threaten, to intimidate, and to silence women. We see technology-facilitated violence in many different forms, including online harassment, cyberstalking, image-based abuse, and other forms of digital violence. Women who step into the public eye, such as politicians, journalists, community leaders, and activists, are particularly exposed and often deliberately targeted. their visibility becomes their vulnerability. And the boundary between the online and physical world is no longer as clear as we might think. A threat made on a screen can quickly become a threat at somebody's door. Abuse that begins online can spill over into the workplace, the home, and the wider community. While this violence can affect anyone, Women are disproportionately targeted, accounting for around 90% of reported victims. When women are driven out of public spaces, we all lose out. We lose ideas, we lose leadership, and we lose perspectives that are essential to building safer and more just societies. This is therefore not just a matter of technology alone. It is a matter of crime prevention and criminal justice. It is a matter of public safety. At its heart, it is a matter of protecting human dignity in a digital world. But because when technology is used to enable violence, the harm is not virtual. It is real. It is a serious violation of human rights. And we must always remember women's rights are human rights. That is why protecting those rights must carry through the entire criminal justice chain. We need to prevent violence before it happens, protect those who are targeted, and hold the perpetrators of this crime to account. Above all, we need to ensure laws, institutions, and capacities can keep up with the rapid pace at which technology itself is evolving. Today's discussion comes at the right time to consider these issues. Across the United Nations system, we are working to build safer, more inclusive digital spaces and to address violence against women and girls. Within our mandate, UNODC is supporting member states to strengthen crime prevention and criminal justice responses, improve support for victims and survivors, and strengthen accountability for tech-enabled forms of violence. For example, as part of our safety initiative, together with experts, we developed a new framework for action on ending technology-facilitated violence against women. The initiative aims to unite the different actors needed to address this challenge, connecting governments, women's protection organizations, first responders, criminal justice institutions, technology companies, civil society and academia to strengthen prevention, protection and accountability. We will work with them to turn commitment into practical action, including by developing tools and guidance that can be adapted to different national and regional realities. We want to help countries learn from one another, strengthen cooperation and build responses that are effective to the changing technological landscape. As part of this effort, we are continuing to advocate for countries to join the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime, which so far has secured close to 100 signatories. We have three ratifications. We need 40 for the instrument to enter into force. For the first time in any international treaty, the non-consensual dissemination of intimate images is recognized as a criminal offense. This represents a major victory for victims of online abuse and an important affirmation that digital violence is real violence. It is also a promise to develop and implement clear legal and operational responses. I therefore encourage all Member States to sign, to ratify and implement this convention and to work collectively to ensure it delivers tangible protection for those most at risk, and particularly women. Beyond the convention, we have also developed a new strategy to prevent and combat non-consensual sharing of intimate images that combines legal, policy, and justice responses with technology-based solutions. And we are ready to go even further. But to do that, we need your support. We need to build closer partnerships, especially with the private sector and tech companies. We need to invest more in prevention, in victim support, and in criminal justice capacities. We need to leverage technology as a force for good and for improving access to justice. And we need international cooperation that reflects the increasingly borderless and transnational nature of online harm. Ladies and gentlemen, women should not have to choose between their safety and participation. Digital spaces should be environments where women can lead, express their views, and contribute confidently and meaningfully to their communities and societies. Let us use this Congress to advance a future in which all women and girls everywhere can participate fully, equally, and safely in public life, both online and offline. I thank you for your kind attention.

Thank you very much. Good morning or good afternoon to you, UN, the OECD and fellow panelists. South Africa welcomes SAFETY as an important initiative and commends the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and the Government of the United Arab Emirates for bringing a renewed international focus to the growing challenge of technology-facilitated violence against women. The safety initiative comes at a critical moment as societies around the world seek to harness the opportunities of a digital age while confronting its emerging risk. Technology has transformed the way we live, work and participate in society. It has expanded access to education, entrepreneurship, justice, public service and political participation. It has enabled women and girls to build businesses, lead institutions, advocate for their communities, connect across borders in an unprecedented ways. However, as digital opportunities have expanded, so too have digital threats. Women and girls are increasingly subjected to online harassment, cyberstalking, image-based abuse, doxing and other forms of technology-facilitated violence that seeks to intimidate, silence and exclude them from public life. This harms and undermines safety, dignity, mental well-being and equal participation in our societies. Excellencies, for South Africa, the issue is particularly significant as the country continues to confront the scourge of gender-based violence and femicide. We therefore recognise that technology-facilitated violence against women is not simply a cybercrime issue, it is a human rights issue. It is an access to justice issue, and it is a developmental issue. Most importantly, it is a challenge to our collective commitment to gender equality and the empowerment of women. South Africa has responded through a combination of legislative reforms, institutional strengthening, and technological innovation. Significant reforms have been undertaken to strengthen protections for victims of gender-based violence and femicide, improve accountability and enhance access to justice. These reforms were specifically designed to close legal gaps, strengthen victim protection and prevent secondary victimization. At the same time, we have embraced technology as an instrument of access to justice. South Africa has introduced online protection order services and electronic repositories for domestic violence protection orders to make justice service more accessible, responsive, and victim-centered. Through the integrated justice system, we continue to modernize and digitize the criminal justice value chain to improve service delivery and ensure that technology serves the interests of victims and communities. However, we are equally conscious that emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence and deepfake technologies, are creating new threats that disproportionately affect women leaders, journalists, public representatives, activists and young women. This development requires the criminal justice system to continuously adapt in innovative and cooperative international and cooperate internationally. South Africa believes that our response must move beyond recognition of the problem towards concrete action. In this regard, South Africa commits itself to five priority areas over and above the ratification of the cyber crime convention and must confirm that we are committed and within the few months we will make sure that this happens because we believe the convention is a critical one and a really timely legal instrument that is needed by the world. From South Africa first, we will continue strengthening our legislative and policy frameworks to ensure that technology-facilitated violence against women is effectively prevented, investigated, prosecuted and punished. The most important thing for us is prevention. Our criminal justice system must evolve as rapidly as the technologies that criminals seek to exploit. Secondly, South Africa will accelerate the digital transformation of the justice sector through IJS to ensure greater accessibility, efficiency, and responsiveness, particularly for women, children, and vulnerable persons seeking justice, but more importantly for people in remote and rural areas, so that we avoid digital divide again as a form of another inequality. Thirdly, We will strengthen specialized support services for victims by improving digital reporting mechanisms, enhancing victim-centered responses, and building the capacity of prosecutors, investigators, magistrates, judges, and specialized courts to address online harms targeting women and girls. This will be in support of our sexual offenses courts that we have established as they remain central to this effort. Fourthly, we will invest in increasing women in science, technology, and engineering and mathematics. Digital literacy, cyber awareness, and online safety initiatives aimed at empowering women and girls to participate confidently, safely, and meaningfully in digital space. Digital inclusion must be accompanied by digital safety. Fifthly, South Africa will continue to strengthen international cooperation, technical assistance and capacity building efforts to combat technology facilitated violence against women and related cyber enabled crimes. No country can address these challenges in isolation effectively. Effective responses require partnerships across governments, international organizations, civil society, and the private technology sector. And this we will do in our period when we are chair of SADC, South African Development Cooperation regions in the southern region, to ensure that all countries can partner within Starting with Africa, expanding to the continent and therefore globally. We therefore welcome the launch of the Safety T Initiative and the Framework for Action on Enabling Technology-Facilitated Violence Against Women as important contributions towards a coherent and coordinated global response. The accompanying digital safety toolkit and global hub for digital safety offer a practical instrument that can assist member states in translating commitments into action. As we navigate the digital age, we must ensure that technological progress advances human dignity, equality, and justice. Women should never be forced to choose between their safety and their participation in public life or digital space. Girls should never have their aspiration diminished by fear of abuse in digital space. Societies cannot achieve inclusive experience.

The real success will be when we no longer think twice about speaking up, when those who have the courage to lead can do so without calculating that the abuse might follow. That means educating men and boys so that they understand the pain that online abuse can cause. And we need to learn to lift women up, not tear them down. Thank you very much, Minister, also for sharing your personal experience and leadership in this area. We now move it to the second part of the event. Thank you very much. I think the first issue tangibly is to make rules and legalise the cyberbullying. Whereas if you train, for example, what we do at the country, the lessons that we've learned around gender-based violence, it was because of different cultures. We had to do training of those that are working in police service, those are working as prosecutors, those are working as presiding officers, and have specialized course and everybody trained to understand. that secondary victimisation is possible and can be done by officials, even officers of court. Thank you very much, minister. I will now turn to Minister Alex Davies-Jones. We cannot do this alone. We need collaboration both across our legal systems, our enforcement agencies, with the tech platforms themselves. So by working in partnership on new legislation, on new regulatory frameworks like we've done in the UK, we have been able to introduce new criminal offences, as I've said, on intimate images, on harmful *********** on tackling really, really illegal abuse online. Because what is illegal offline should be illegal online. There is no blur, there's no distinction anymore between the online and offline world. We all live in an ever more connected world and therefore our laws have to keep up at that pace to evolve to work with them. But that also means that law enforcement, our police, needs to be able to catch up and be educated and trained in response to this, working with our judiciary on their training and then victim support as well-being able to highlight where that is. Because what I would say is something we have seen in the United Kingdom is that where these crimes occur online, they very really stay online. They will follow into the offline world. They do cause real-world harm. A lot of people have said, "Oh, it's not real. It's happening online." But it does have a huge impact on the victims and on society, and that's why we need to tackle it.
